title: Signal Lost
author: Léxi
desc: Kevin, jeune informaticien d'une société de mobile money à Abidjan, découvre que des milliers de petits comptes perdent quelques francs chaque nuit. Qui vole les pauvres, centime par centime ?

p: Kevin Yao was not supposed to be looking at the night transactions. His job at FlashPay, one of the fastest-growing mobile money companies in Côte d'Ivoire, was to make the app load faster. He was twenty-six, he had graduated top of his class from the engineering school in Yamoussoukro, and he spent most of his days trying to shave milliseconds off a screen that showed people their balance.

He noticed the anomaly by accident, on a Tuesday night when the office was empty and he was testing a new database query. Between two and four a.m., several thousand accounts had each lost a tiny amount of money. Forty-seven francs here. Ninety-two there. Never more than a hundred.

The amounts were so small that nobody would ever complain. Who checks their mobile money balance at four in the morning to discover that ninety francs have vanished? But Kevin did the multiplication on a piece of paper, and his pen stopped moving.
Across two million accounts, every night, it added up to roughly sixty million francs a month.
Someone was stealing from the poorest customers in the country, one coin at a time.

The money did not disappear completely. It was routed, through a chain of eleven intermediate accounts, into a single business account registered to a company called Lumière Services SARL. The company had an address in Marcory, a tax number and absolutely no online presence.

Kevin knew he should report it to his manager. But something stopped him. The code that moved the money was not an external hack; it was inside FlashPay's own system, hidden in a routine maintenance script that ran every night. Whoever had written it had administrator access — and there were only six people in the company with that level of access.
His manager, Patricia Ehouman, was one of them.

He spent the weekend reading the code line by line. The author had been careful: no names, no comments, no obvious mistakes. But programmers, like writers, have habits. This one used a particular way of naming variables — always in French, always with a small joke. A variable called *petit_poisson*. Another called *la_mer_est_grande*.

Kevin had seen that style before. He opened the company's code history and searched for "poisson". There were exactly two authors who used it. One was Patricia. The other was the company's founder and CEO, Armand Kacou.
He decided to trust Patricia. It was, he later admitted, a calculation as much as a feeling: if she was guilty, he was already in trouble; if she was innocent, he needed her.
He showed her the numbers in a noisy café in the Plateau, far from the office. She read in silence for twenty minutes. Then she put down the laptop, very carefully, as if it might explode.

"I wrote *petit_poisson*," she said quietly. "Four years ago. It was a function to round transaction fees. Armand asked me to write it. He said it was for accounting." She closed her eyes. "Someone took my code and changed it. Someone who knew my style well enough to hide behind it."
"So if this comes out—"
"It will look like me," she finished. "Exactly. Which is probably the point."

They needed proof that couldn't be faked: who had modified the script, from which computer, at what time. The logs existed, Patricia said, but they were stored on a secure server that only the CEO could access directly.

"Or," she added slowly, "someone who knows the backup password. Which changes every month. And which the CEO writes on a yellow sticky note under his keyboard, because he's convinced nobody would ever think of looking there."

The FlashPay office occupied the top two floors of a glass tower in the Plateau. On Friday night, the security guard knew Kevin well — he was always the last to leave — and waved him through without a second look.

Patricia had the CEO's schedule: he was in Accra until Sunday. His office was locked, but the cleaning staff left the door open on Fridays while they mopped the floor. Kevin waited in the stairwell until he heard the trolley rattle away down the corridor.
The yellow sticky note was exactly where she had said.

It took him nine minutes to download the logs onto an encrypted drive and four minutes more to understand what they showed. Every modification to the nightly script had been made from a single laptop, registered to Armand Kacou, between midnight and one a.m., always on a Friday.
He was copying the last file when the lift arrived on the top floor with a soft electronic ping.
Kevin switched off the screen and dropped behind the desk. Footsteps crossed the open-plan office — slow, heavy, confident. They stopped just outside the glass door.
Through the gap under the desk, he saw a pair of expensive brown shoes. He recognised them immediately. Every employee did.
The CEO had not gone to Accra after all.
Armand Kacou sat down on the sofa by the window, took out his phone and made a call. He spoke in a low, irritated voice.

"No, I told you. Friday is the last time. After that we stop... Because the boy in development is asking questions, that's why. Patricia's name is all over the code — if anything happens, it's her... Yes. Lumière closes on Monday. Transfer everything to the Dubai account tonight."
He hung up and sat staring at the city lights for what felt like an hour. It was eleven minutes. Then he left.
Kevin did not move until he heard the lift doors close. His hands were shaking so much that it took him three attempts to unplug the drive.

On Monday morning, the logs, the recording he had made on his phone, and a seventy-page report were on the desks of the Central Bank's financial crimes unit and of a journalist at *Fraternité Matin*. The money in the Lumière account was frozen before it reached Dubai.
Armand Kacou was arrested at the airport on Wednesday, on his way to Accra — for real, this time.

Two months later, two million FlashPay customers received an unexpected text message: *A refund has been credited to your account.* Most of them were puzzled by the amount. Forty-seven francs. Ninety-two. Sometimes a few thousand.
Kevin, now head of security at FlashPay, received one too. Three hundred and twelve francs. He never found out how they had taken it from him. He had it framed anyway.
